precepts.text: Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity. What is the putting forth of the finger? That is blaming. He blamed the people. So King Saul blamed the people right after saying that he kept Agag alive. So you are blaming the people for keeping the sheep and the best of the flocks, but you did not take accountability for keeping Agag the Amalekite alive. So what did the Lord say? He is not going to hear any of us until we stop playing the blame game. Stop blaming others. How are you dealing with that situation? Oh, I am bitter against this person because they did this to me. I have hatred towards this person because of this. The Lord does not care about your reasoning. I am going to tell you that right now. The Lord does not care about your reasoning or your justification, because every one of us will be judged according to our ways. The Lord sees how that person is treating you. The same way the Lord sees how you are reacting to that treatment. The Lord sees it. So if you trust in the Lord you are going to act according to how God commanded you to deal with that situation, and then let the Lord deal with that person.
precepts.point: But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

precepts.why:
Samuel asked Saul, “Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord?” King Saul had an issue with being obedient to the Lord, and God called that disobedience evil in his sight. Saul answered, “Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the Lord”, and then, “But the people took of the spoil.” Was that a sign of godly sorrow? No, there was none involved. Isaiah 58:9 names what Saul was doing.

“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity.”

What is the putting forth of the finger? That is blaming. Saul blamed the people right after saying he had kept Agag alive. He blamed the people for keeping the sheep and the best of the flocks, but did not take accountability for keeping Agag the Amalekite alive. So what does the Lord say? He is not going to hear any of us until we stop playing the blame game. The Lord answers, “Here I am”, when the finger is taken away.

Stop blaming others. How are you dealing with that situation? I am bitter against this person because they did this to me; I have hatred towards this person because of this. The Lord does not care about your reasoning or your justification, because every one of us will be judged according to our ways. The Lord sees how that person is treating you, and the same way he sees how you are reacting to that treatment. If you trust in the Lord, you act according to how God commanded you to deal with that situation, and then let the Lord deal with that person.

That is a building block of bitterness. Disobedience, then justifying yourself, then blaming others: the bitterness is compounded on sins that were already there. As 1 Samuel 15:22 says, “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.”

precepts.text: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression.
precepts.point: The burden of Babylon which Isaiah saw: lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, the government, America; the banner is the Bible. Exalt the voice unto them, as Isaiah 58:1 says lift it up like a trumpet and spare not, and shake the hand, warn our people, that they may go into the gates of the nobles. In the midst of the war Isaiah sees the prophets still going out.

note.label: America At War With Iran: Preparation For Conflict

precepts.why:
“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see. Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand.” The high mountain is the government, America. The banner we lift up upon it is the Bible. So in the midst of all this chaos, Isaiah sees the prophets still going out teaching.

“Exalt the voice unto them”: that is what we do, and Isaiah 58 says how. “Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.” We exalt the voice, we spare not, we lift up our voice as a trumpet.

“Shake the hand”: warn our people, “that they may go into the gates of the nobles.” The nations have drunk Babylon's wine, her lies and philosophies, what Daniel calls her policy, and therefore the nations are mad. War is coming, and in the midst of all that war, the prophets are still crying aloud, showing our people their transgression so they can be saved.

precepts.text: The fast that the Lord has chosen is a day for a man to afflict his soul, to loose the bands of wickedness, and to break every yoke.
precepts.point: Isaiah 53 cannot be speaking of David, who was already dead in Isaiah's day; it speaks of Jesus Christ, cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of the people, the ultimate sacrifice.

note.label: Numbers 29: The Feasts of the Seventh Month

precepts.why:
“ye shall afflict your souls.” To afflict your soul is to fast. “Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?”

“Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?” The fast the Lord has chosen is a day for a man to afflict his soul, to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke.

That is why we still fast on this day once a year, and why we go out and teach on the day of atonement.

precepts.text: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet; the spirit of the great shout at the wall.
precepts.point: The people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city and utterly destroyed all that was in it, both man and woman, young and old, ox, sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
“So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat”. That shout is Isaiah 58:1 in action: “Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.”

The sound coming out of their mouths with the trumpets broke everything down, like thousands of lions roaring at once. Lift up thy voice like a trumpet: that is the spirit of the great shout at the wall, and the wall came down flat so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and took it.

precepts.text: Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer, if thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke and the putting forth of the finger; the Most High says stop playing the blame game if you want him to intervene on your behalf, but pointing the finger is exactly what Saul did.
precepts.point: Samuel asks, What hast thou done? Saul answers with excuses: the people were scattered from me, thou camest not within the days appointed, the Philistines gathered at Michmash, so I forced myself and offered a burnt offering. This is part of Saul's pattern of behavior; he never wants to hold himself accountable, he always deflects onto whoever else.

note.label: 1 Samuel 13: Make Not Haste in Time of Trouble

precepts.why:
Samuel asks, “What hast thou done?” and Saul answers with excuses: “Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that thou camest not within the days appointed, and that the Philistines gathered themselves together at Michmash”, so “I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.” This is part of Saul’s pattern of behavior: he never wants to hold himself accountable; he always deflects onto whoever else.

“Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity”. The Most High says stop playing the blame game if you want him to intervene on your behalf. Pointing the finger is exactly what Saul did.

precepts.text: The fast the Most High chooses is a day to afflict the soul before him.
precepts.point: Ezra was ashamed to require of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help against the enemy in the way, having testified that the hand of God is upon all who seek him for good.

note.label: Ezra 8: The Company Returns And Fasts At Ahava

precepts.why:
Ezra “proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God.” To afflict the soul is to fast, taking neither food nor water. Isaiah puts the fast and the affliction together: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?”

The fast the Most High chooses is a day to afflict the soul before him. That is what Ezra's company did at Ahava: they afflicted themselves before their God “to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance.” One may fast and pray for wisdom and a right path, as they did.
